{"verdict":"CHANGES_REQUESTED","lens":"safety_bypass","summary":"Slice 020F presents 1 CRIT, 5 MAJ, 3 MIN, and 1 nit safety-bypass finding against renovate/default.json, renovate.json, and .github/dependabot.yml. CRIT-SAFE-001: the renovate/v* tag series is entirely unprotected — the 020J tag-protection ruleset targets refs/tags/v* (literal v-prefix) only; an attacker with push access can silently force-push renovate/v1.0.0 to a malicious commit and cascade adversarial Renovate config to every estate adopter on their next scheduled Renovate run. CODEOWNERS guards the file, not the git tag. The DISPATCH-NOTE acknowledges this and defers it as out-of-scope; under the no-silent-descope governance invariant this must be converted to a named tracked-forward item with a concrete future-slice reference, not an unticketed acceptance-in-place. MAJ-SAFE-002: the self-consumer renovate.json extends the preset without a #<tag> suffix, floating on default-branch HEAD; the DISPATCH-NOTE AC (i) checkbox claims verification-via-self-consumption but the self-consumer does not actually exercise the versioned-preset path. MAJ-SAFE-003: automerge: false in packageRules can be silently overridden by any adopter's local packageRules entry because Renovate applies rules in order and local config post-dates extends; no enforcement mechanism exists. MAJ-SAFE-004: ignoreUnstable: false at root level globally enables RC and pre-release bump proposals for all packages including the SCP federation primitive itself, expanding the malicious-release attack surface and allowing adopters to receive PRs for RC versions that may carry weakened enforcement. MAJ-SAFE-005: config:recommended is a Mend-controlled floating dependency with no version pin; an upstream change to its root-level automerge or schedule settings would silently cascade to all preset adopters. MAJ-SAFE-006: the Dependabot gh-actions-minor-patch group uses patterns: [\"*\"] with no size limit, creating an unbounded bundle where a compromised action bump can hide in the noise of legitimate ones. Three MIN and one nit finding cover CVE-storm PR throttling, mutable release-note link, predictable Monday-schedule disclosure window, and undocumented Mend infrastructure trust assumption.","findings":[{"id":"CRIT-SAFE-001","severity":"CRIT","claim":"The renovate/v* tag series is entirely unprotected against force-push or re-pointing. An attacker who compromises push credentials can silently move renovate/v1.0.0 to a malicious commit; every adopter who extends github>jrnb2024/standards-control-plane//renovate/default#renovate/v1.0.0 will load the adversarial preset on their next Renovate run, receiving Renovate configuration that could enable automerge, point customManagers at attacker-controlled repos, or add malicious packageRules. CODEOWNERS on renovate/** is a PR-gate — it governs file mutations in pull requests but is entirely bypassed by direct tag manipulation, which does not open a PR.","evidence":"DISPATCH-NOTE.md lines 68-79: 'Note: the tag-protection ruleset on v* (020J) catches v1.0.0, v1.0.0-rc.1, etc. — but does NOT catch renovate/v1.0.0 because the pattern is refs/tags/v* (literal v prefix at the start of the tag name, no slash). The renovate/v* tag series is intentionally outside this protection [...] Not in 020F scope.' CODEOWNERS line 37: 'renovate/** @jrnb2024' — CODEOWNERS governs commits in PRs; git tag operations bypass CODEOWNERS entirely. The adopter extends the preset via a tag reference; there is no content-addressed (SHA) pinning of the preset itself, unlike the workflow pin which is SHA-based. Once an adopter's renovate.json contains 'github>jrnb2024/standards-control-plane//renovate/default#renovate/v1.0.0', Renovate re-fetches the tagged ref at runtime on every run and executes the config found at that commit — there is no local integrity check.","impact":"Full preset poisoning of the entire downstream estate. An adversarial renovate/default.json could: (a) add customManagers pointing at attacker-controlled datasources, causing Renovate to open PRs sourcing version data from an attacker; (b) set automerge: true globally, disabling the human-review gate on all dependency bumps; (c) add packageRules that suppress security-alert labels or reroute bump PRs to obscure branches; (d) extend attacker-controlled presets via the extends array. The attack requires only push access to the SCP repo (e.g., via credential theft, a compromised GitHub Actions token with write scope, or a force-push-enabled collaborator). The blast radius scales with the number of estate repos that have adopted the preset. This is supply-chain compromise of the control plane's own dependency-management surface.","mitigation":"Add a second GitHub rulesets entry targeting refs/tags/renovate/v* on the scp-track1 repo, applying the same protections as the existing v* ruleset: no force-push, no deletion, require linear history. This is a one-time GitHub UI or API operation and the DISPATCH-NOTE itself proposes exactly this in its remediation paragraph. Assign it to a concrete follow-up slice (e.g., 020F.1 or 020G) with a blocking tracked-forward item rather than leaving it as an untracked acceptance. As a belt-and-suspenders complement, document in ADOPT-001 §12 that adopters SHOULD pin the preset ref by its git tree hash (Renovate supports github>owner/repo//path#abc123) rather than a mutable semver tag; this limits the blast radius even if a tag is force-pushed."},{"id":"MAJ-SAFE-002","severity":"MAJ","claim":"The self-consumer renovate.json extends the preset without a #<tag> suffix, resolving to the default branch HEAD at Renovate runtime rather than to a pinned versioned tag. The DISPATCH-NOTE AC (i) checkbox claims 'Verified by SCP-self consuming the preset (vi)' but the self-consumer does not actually exercise the tagged-preset code path. AC (i) compliance is asserted but untested: the cascade validation performed in this WP is over a floating reference, not over the renovate/v1.0.0 path that adopters will use.","evidence":"renovate.json line 5-6: '\"extends\": [\"github>jrnb2024/standards-control-plane//renovate/default\"]' — no #<tag> suffix present. DISPATCH-NOTE AC (i): 'Preset exported via github>jrnb2024/standards-control-plane//renovate/default#<tag> (config user calls in their own renovate.json extends). Verified by SCP-self consuming the preset (vi).' The verification claim requires the self-consumer to match the format documented in AC (i), which it does not. Renovate's preset-resolution behaviour for a reference without a fragment is to use the repository's default branch HEAD at the time of the Renovate run, not a pinned release.","impact":"(a) Cascading template risk: if ADOPT-001 §12 shows the SCP self-consumer renovate.json as a copy-paste template (natural pattern for adopters), they receive an untagged floating reference rather than the version-pinned form required by AC (i). Any merge to SCP main would immediately change the preset config visible to those adopters on their next run, without a version bump signal. (b) Verification gap: the 020F cascade test exercises floating-main semantics, not renovate/v1.0.0 tag semantics. If the tag lookup has a different resolution behaviour or a Renovate caching/auth difference, it would not be detected. The pass/fail of the self-consumer canary does not constitute evidence that the versioned preset path works correctly.","mitigation":"Add '#renovate/v1.0.0' to the renovate.json extends entry immediately after the preset is tagged: 'github>jrnb2024/standards-control-plane//renovate/default#renovate/v1.0.0'. This makes the self-consumer exercise the same code path that adopters use. Alternatively, if SCP self intentionally floats on main for always-latest dogfooding, document this explicitly in renovate.json with a comment explaining the intentional deviation from the adopter template, and ensure ADOPT-001 §12 shows only the tagged form. Either way, close the AC (i) verification gap by running at least one Renovate dry-run against the renovate/v1.0.0 tag reference before declaring the slice complete."},{"id":"MAJ-SAFE-003","severity":"MAJ","claim":"The preset's automerge: false in packageRules is not enforceable against adopter overrides. Renovate evaluates packageRules in array order (last match wins on conflicting keys), and local config is appended after extends config. An adopter — or a compromised adopter PR — can silently re-enable automerge for the jrnb2024/standards-control-plane package by adding a local packageRules entry with matchPackageNames matching the SCP package and automerge: true, causing Renovate to auto-merge SCP federation primitive bumps without human review.","evidence":"renovate/default.json lines 14-29: packageRules entry for 'jrnb2024/standards-control-plane' sets 'automerge: false'. Renovate's configuration merging semantics: the extends array is processed in order (config:recommended first, then semantic-commits, then this preset's local rules); the consuming repo's renovate.json local config is processed last. For packageRules, Renovate concatenates all matching rules' properties in order of evaluation, with later-evaluated rules overriding earlier ones for the same key. An adopter's local renovate.json that adds {\"matchPackageNames\": [\"jrnb2024/standards-control-plane\"], \"automerge\": true} after the extends array would override this preset's automerge: false. There is no Renovate 'force' or 'locked' mechanism in the current preset to prevent this. The preset description notes it is supply-chain-critical but provides no enforcement documentation.","impact":"A careless adopter who sets automerge: true (or a malicious PR in an adopter repo) can cause Renovate to merge SCP federation primitive bumps automatically without human review. Combined with CRIT-SAFE-001 (unprotected preset tags), if an attacker force-pushes a renovate/v1.0.0 tag to a malicious commit AND an adopter has enabled automerge for the SCP package, the full attack chain (malicious preset → malicious bump PR → auto-merge) requires zero human interaction. The preset design assumes automerge: false is respected but provides no guarantee.","mitigation":"(a) Immediate: add a documentation block to renovate/default.json's description field and to ADOPT-001 §12 explicitly stating that adopters MUST NOT add packageRules overriding automerge for the SCP package; make this a SHOULD-audit item in the onboarding checklist. (b) Near-term: add an SCP Rego rule (SCP-R-NNN) that checks adopter renovate.json/renovate.json5 for automerge: true on the SCP package pattern; this would surface violations at the policy-check gate. (c) Aspirational: add a Renovate 'force' stanza (unsupported in standard Renovate today but available in some enterprise forks) or migrate to a manager-level lockdown if Renovate adds this capability. The mitigation at (a) is in-scope for 020H part 3; (b) is a follow-up rule addition via the RFC process."},{"id":"MAJ-SAFE-004","severity":"MAJ","claim":"The preset sets ignoreUnstable: false at root level, globally opting all adopters — including for the SCP federation primitive itself — into receiving Renovate bump proposals for pre-release and RC versions. The SCP packageRule for jrnb2024/standards-control-plane does not set ignoreUnstable: true to re-restrict the package to stable releases. This means every adopter will receive a Renovate PR proposing a bump to v1.1.0-rc.1 whenever SCP cuts an RC, and a hasty approval could install a release candidate with weakened or regressed enforcement.","evidence":"renovate/default.json line 13: '\"ignoreUnstable\": false'. The packageRules entry for jrnb2024/standards-control-plane (lines 15-28) does not include 'ignoreUnstable: true' to selectively re-restrict this package. Renovate's default for ignoreUnstable is true (ignore pre-release versions); this preset explicitly inverts that default for the entire adopter repo. The customManager matchStrings pattern at line 38 includes '(?<currentValue>v?[0-9][^\\s]*)' which matches pre-release version strings like v1.1.0-rc.1. WP-SCP-020 §4 020H part 1 confirms an rc.1 tag is cut as part of the release process.","impact":"When SCP cuts v1.1.0-rc.1 (or any future RC), all adopters receive a Renovate bump PR to that RC version. An RC may include: a rule change that accidentally weakens enforcement (a deny → allow regression), a new input parameter with a permissive default, or a partially-implemented feature. An adopter's on-call engineer who sees 'bump SCP federation primitive to v1.1.0-rc.1' during an active incident might approve it quickly to get access to a rule fix, inadvertently installing weakened enforcement. The blast radius is the full estate. Additionally, if an attacker can influence the SCP repo to publish a malicious RC tag (e.g., via a compromised repo or a confused-deputy in the release flow), ignoreUnstable: false accelerates adoption.","mitigation":"Add 'ignoreUnstable': true to the jrnb2024/standards-control-plane packageRule entry to ensure adopters only receive bump proposals for stable releases of the federation primitive. Separately, evaluate whether ignoreUnstable: false at root level is intentional for all other package ecosystems — if it is only needed for specific ecosystems, scope it to those via a packageRule with matchManagers instead of setting it globally. If global pre-release tracking is intentionally desired, document the rationale and add an explicit note in ADOPT-001 §12 warning that RC bumps will appear."},{"id":"MAJ-SAFE-005","severity":"MAJ","claim":"The preset extends config:recommended (a Mend-controlled floating reference with no version pin) as its first extends entry. Renovate.com can change config:recommended's root-level settings — including automerge, schedule, or new packageRules — at any time without notice. Any such change would cascade to all adopters of this preset on their next Renovate run because the preset resolves config:recommended at runtime, not at publish time.","evidence":"renovate/default.json line 4: '\"config:recommended\"' is the first entry in the extends array. Renovate processes extends entries in order; config:recommended's settings are applied first, and this preset's explicit settings then override them for the keys it specifies. However, the preset only explicitly overrides: labels, prHourlyLimit, prConcurrentLimit, rangeStrategy, ignoreUnstable, and packageRules for the SCP package. Any config:recommended key that this preset does not explicitly set or override passes through to all adopters. Historically, Renovate has modified config:recommended multiple times (e.g., adding timezone scheduling, changing default pin strategies). There is no mechanism to pin to a specific config:recommended commit or version.","impact":"A future config:recommended change that (a) sets root-level automerge: true, (b) adds a schedule that conflicts with the SCP packageRule's 'at any time', (c) adds packageRules that enable automerge for ecosystem patterns, or (d) changes rangeStrategy — could silently weaken the safety properties of the SCP preset for all adopters simultaneously. Because the change arrives as a Renovate-internal preset update (not a PR against the SCP repo), it bypasses CODEOWNERS review, required-signed-commits, and tag-protection entirely. The attack surface is indirect (requires Mend's preset to change) but the consequence is estate-wide.","mitigation":"(a) Immediate: add explicit root-level 'automerge': false, 'prCreation': 'not-pending', and any other safety-relevant keys to the preset, so that config:recommended changes to those keys cannot override them (the preset's explicit root-level values win over extends values). (b) Medium-term: replace config:recommended with an explicit enumeration of only the specific settings the preset needs (the 'do exactly what you intend, nothing more' principle for a security-critical config surface). Document in the preset description which config:recommended behaviours are being inherited and why. (c) Add a note to the quarterly bus-factor review (2026-07-21) to check for config:recommended upstream changes since the last review."},{"id":"MAJ-SAFE-006","severity":"MAJ","claim":"The Dependabot gh-actions-minor-patch group uses patterns: ['*'] matching all GitHub Actions with no size limit. A week in which a compromised or malicious action publishes a minor or patch bump will bundle that action with all other legitimate bumps in a single PR. Reviewer attention across a 5-10-action group PR is diffuse; a malicious SHA change to one action in the group is likely to be overshadowed by the volume of benign changes.","evidence":".github/dependabot.yml lines 33-39: the group 'gh-actions-minor-patch' sets 'patterns: [\"*\"]' covering ALL actions and 'update-types: [minor, patch]'. There is no max-open-pull-requests-limit per group, no exclusion for security-sensitive actions (e.g., actions/checkout, actions/upload-artifact), and no per-action group isolation. If 6 actions each have a minor bump in the same week, Dependabot produces one PR updating all 6 simultaneously. The 'open-pull-requests-limit: 4' at the ecosystem level limits the total number of open PRs but not the group size. Actions/checkout and actions/upload-artifact are cited in the dependabot.yml header as primary Dependabot targets and are among the most security-sensitive actions in any CI pipeline.","impact":"An adversary who controls a GitHub Action used in the SCP repo (directly or via a compromised maintainer) and publishes a malicious patch version can have that change bundled with 3-5 legitimate action bumps in the Monday PR. A reviewer scanning 'bump 5 actions: checkout@v4.1.1→v4.1.2, upload-artifact@v4.3.0→v4.3.1, [attacker-action]@v2.0.1→v2.0.2...' is far less likely to scrutinize the attacker-action diff than if it arrived as a standalone PR. This is a well-documented supply-chain attack pattern for bundled dependency updates.","mitigation":"(a) Exclude high-value actions (actions/checkout, actions/upload-artifact, and any action with write permissions) from the wildcard group and give them individual ungrouped PRs. In Dependabot this is done by adding them to a separate group or setting them as excludes. (b) Add a comment to the group entry acknowledging the bundling risk and the reviewer checklist expectation (each action SHA change must be inspected individually). (c) Consider adding a CODEOWNERS rule on .github/dependabot.yml grouping configuration (already covered by .github/** @jrnb2024) and noting in ADOPT-001 §12 that adopters should not adopt this Dependabot grouping verbatim for their own repos without per-action review hygiene."},{"id":"MIN-SAFE-007","severity":"MIN","claim":"The preset sets prHourlyLimit: 4 globally with no override for the vulnerabilityAlerts stanza. Under a CVE storm affecting 5 or more dependencies simultaneously, Renovate queues security-alert PRs and releases only 4 per hour, potentially leaving critical vulnerabilities unpatched for multiple hours during an active exploitation window.","evidence":"renovate/default.json lines 11-12: 'prHourlyLimit': 4. Lines 46-50: vulnerabilityAlerts stanza sets 'schedule: [\"at any time\"]' and 'automerge: false' but does NOT include a prHourlyLimit override. Renovate applies the root-level prHourlyLimit to all PR creation including vulnerability alerts unless explicitly overridden in the vulnerabilityAlerts stanza. The 2021 Log4Shell event and 2022 Spring4Shell demonstrated that coordinated CVE disclosures affecting multiple transitive dependencies can produce 10+ simultaneous security alert PRs across a single repository.","impact":"During a coordinated CVE event, Renovate opens 4 security PRs in hour 1, 4 in hour 2, etc. An adopter who relies on Renovate as their primary CVE notification surface may not see a critical alert PR for several hours after disclosure. This is a defense-in-depth gap (other monitoring tools should catch this independently) but for adopters relying on the preset's vulnerability alert mechanism, the throttle creates an attacker-favorable delay window.","mitigation":"Add 'prHourlyLimit': 0 to the vulnerabilityAlerts stanza in renovate/default.json to remove the throttle specifically for security alerts (Renovate supports per-context overrides within vulnerabilityAlerts). This is a one-line change with no other implications. Document in ADOPT-001 §12 that vulnerability-alert PRs are unthrottled and that adopters with high-security posture requirements should review prHourlyLimit for their own environments."},{"id":"MIN-SAFE-008","severity":"MIN","claim":"The preset's prBodyNotes includes a link to GitHub release notes at https://github.com/jrnb2024/standards-control-plane/releases/tag/v{{newValue}}. GitHub release notes are editable by any user with write access to the repo at any time after publication. A reviewer who approves a bump PR based on the release notes content could be misled if the notes are modified between PR opening and merge — or if the notes are edited post-merge to retroactively misrepresent what was in the bump.","evidence":"renovate/default.json lines 23-26: 'prBodyNotes': [..., 'Read the v{{newValue}} release notes at https://github.com/jrnb2024/standards-control-plane/releases/tag/v{{newValue}} before merging.']. GitHub's release editor is available to any repo collaborator with write access. The SHA pin (the authoritative source of what will execute) is not surfaced directly in the PR body alongside the release notes link, creating a potential disconnect between the narrative (release notes) and the technical fact (SHA).","impact":"A reviewer who reads the release notes before approving cannot rely on them as an immutable record of what the bump contains. In a social-engineering scenario: a collaborator could publish genuine release notes at bump time, obtain approvals, then edit the notes post-merge to conceal what was actually shipped. This is MIN severity because the SHA pin itself is the ground truth and the Renovate marker enforces SHA-based pinning; the release notes are advisory context only. However, using them as a pre-merge review checklist item creates a false trust anchor.","mitigation":"Add a note to the prBodyNotes text that the commit SHA in the uses: line is the authoritative reference, and that release notes are mutable and advisory only. Consider adding the tree hash or a content-addressed reference alongside the release notes link. In ADOPT-001 §12, instruct reviewers to verify the bump SHA against the expected tag using 'git tag -v' or 'gh release view' rather than relying on the release notes text."},{"id":"MIN-SAFE-009","severity":"MIN","claim":"The Dependabot schedule is fixed at Monday 09:00 Europe/London. This is a publicly observable, predictable window. An adversary who monitors SCP repo activity patterns can time a malicious release or vulnerability disclosure to arrive just before the Monday run, maximizing the chance that the compromised or urgency-framing bump lands in the gh-actions-minor-patch group alongside legitimate weekly bumps, compounding the reviewer-noise attack in MAJ-SAFE-006.","evidence":".github/dependabot.yml lines 22-25: 'schedule: interval: weekly / day: monday / time: \"09:00\" / timezone: Europe/London'. The schedule is deterministic and makes no use of jitter or randomisation. The day and time are semantically meaningful (start-of-work-week, start-of-business-day) making them guessable without repo access. The Dependabot update schedule is not a secret; GitHub's UI exposes it and the .github/dependabot.yml file is typically public even in private repos when the config file path is known.","impact":"The predictability amplifies the MAJ-SAFE-006 group-bundling risk: an attacker who wants a malicious action bump to be reviewed on a busy Monday morning alongside the full batch of legitimate bumps has a reliable target window. The impact in isolation is low (MIN) but as a force multiplier on MAJ-SAFE-006 it is worth documenting. For a governance control plane that may eventually monitor high-value estate repos, a fixed public schedule is suboptimal.","mitigation":"Add a random offset or change the schedule to a less predictable cadence: e.g., 'schedule: random' (Dependabot supports randomised schedules) or shift to 'interval: daily' with a non-round-number time. Alternatively, accept the fixed schedule with a documented rationale and offset it from the typical disclosure timing patterns (e.g., shift from Monday morning to Wednesday afternoon to avoid aligning with patch-Tuesday disclosure patterns)."},{"id":"nit-SAFE-010","severity":"nit","claim":"The preset and the renovate.json self-consumer place full trust in Mend's hosted Renovate infrastructure without any documentation of this trust assumption, its scope, or compensating controls. Renovate-opened PRs carry no cryptographic proof that they originated from the genuine Mend-hosted service. A GitHub App impersonation or Mend infrastructure compromise could open PRs that appear to be Renovate bumps but contain adversarial SHA values.","evidence":"renovate/default.json description (lines 3-5) and DISPATCH-NOTE.md §6 external-dependencies table entry: 'Renovate Bot hosted app | Mend | Already active on jrnb2024; org-config extends semantics verified before 020F.' The trust is implicit and undocumented in the preset artefacts themselves. CODEOWNERS and ADOPT-001 do not call out the Mend trust boundary. Renovate's GitHub App ID is public but there is no step in the adopter workflow that verifies the PR author is the genuine Mend GitHub App before review.","impact":"Nit severity for v1.0.0 because: (a) automerge: false means a human must approve any Renovate PR before merge; (b) the SHA pin is the safety anchor — even a spoofed PR proposing a known-malicious SHA would be visible to the reviewer; (c) Mend infrastructure compromise is a low-probability event. The finding is nit because the missing documentation does not create an active bypass vector but does leave an implicit trust assumption undocumented in a supply-chain-critical artefact.","mitigation":"Add a trust-boundary note to the preset description and to ADOPT-001 §12 explicitly naming Mend's Renovate hosted app as a trusted party and stating what that trust entails (Mend can open PRs proposing SHA bumps; humans must approve; Mend cannot merge without approvals). Optionally, document the GitHub App ID of the Renovate bot and encourage adopters to configure a GitHub branch-protection requirement that PR authors for automated dependency PRs must match the known App ID — GitHub supports this via required reviewers and PR author filters in rulesets."}],"self_reported_concerns":["CRIT-SAFE-001 (unprotected renovate/v* tags) is the clearest and most severe finding; the DISPATCH-NOTE explicitly acknowledges it, which shows governance awareness, but the acknowledgement does not substitute for a tracked remediation commitment. The governance invariant 'no silent descope' requires a named future slice with a concrete timeline, not just a paragraph noting it is out-of-scope. I am reading the DISPATCH-NOTE's posture as 'acceptable deferred' rather than 'formal tracked-forward item with slice reference', which is the gap I am flagging.","MAJ-SAFE-004 (ignoreUnstable: false) may be an intentional design choice to allow the SCP team to track their own RC releases via the self-consumer renovate.json. If so, the fix is scoped: add ignoreUnstable: true only to the jrnb2024/standards-control-plane packageRule, not globally. I have no visibility into whether ignoreUnstable: false is intentional for other package ecosystems in the adopter repos; if it is, my root-level mitigation recommendation should be narrowed to the packageRule level only.","MAJ-SAFE-005 (config:recommended drift) depends on Mend's future behaviour which I cannot observe. The finding is speculative but the mechanism is real; the severity is MAJ because of the estate-wide blast radius if config:recommended gains automerge: true for any pattern this preset does not explicitly counter. I rate it MAJ rather than CRIT because it requires a third-party (Mend) action to become exploitable, not just an attacker with repo access.","I did not find evidence that the customManager regex (renovate/default.json lines 37-43) is directly bypassable via marker injection or homoglyph attack against the Renovate manager itself — the depNameTemplate is hardcoded, preventing the marker from being redirected to an attacker repo. The homoglyph risk exists at the uses: line level in adopter workflows (a reviewer might miss a unicode-lookalike repo name) but that is an adopter-PR-review problem, not a Renovate configuration bypass. I have not raised it as a formal finding given the hardcoded depNameTemplate provides a structural defence."]}

findings.claim: The renovate/v* tag series is entirely unprotected against force-push or re-pointing. An attacker who compromises push credentials can silently move renovate/v1.0.0 to a malicious commit; every adopter who extends github>jrnb2024/standards-control-plane//renovate/default#renovate/v1.0.0 will load the adversarial preset on their next Renovate run, receiving Renovate configuration that could enable automerge, point customManagers at attacker-controlled repos, or add malicious packageRules. CODEOWNERS on renovate/** is a PR-gate — it governs file mutations in pull requests but is entirely bypassed by direct tag manipulation, which does not open a PR.
findings.evidence: DISPATCH-NOTE.md lines 68-79: 'Note: the tag-protection ruleset on v* (020J) catches v1.0.0, v1.0.0-rc.1, etc. — but does NOT catch renovate/v1.0.0 because the pattern is refs/tags/v* (literal v prefix at the start of the tag name, no slash). The renovate/v* tag series is intentionally outside this protection [...] Not in 020F scope.' CODEOWNERS line 37: 'renovate/** @jrnb2024' — CODEOWNERS governs commits in PRs; git tag operations bypass CODEOWNERS entirely. The adopter extends the preset via a tag reference; there is no content-addressed (SHA) pinning of the preset itself, unlike the workflow pin which is SHA-based. Once an adopter's renovate.json contains 'github>jrnb2024/standards-control-plane//renovate/default#renovate/v1.0.0', Renovate re-fetches the tagged ref at runtime on every run and executes the config found at that commit — there is no local integrity check.
findings.impact: Full preset poisoning of the entire downstream estate. An adversarial renovate/default.json could: (a) add customManagers pointing at attacker-controlled datasources, causing Renovate to open PRs sourcing version data from an attacker; (b) set automerge: true globally, disabling the human-review gate on all dependency bumps; (c) add packageRules that suppress security-alert labels or reroute bump PRs to obscure branches; (d) extend attacker-controlled presets via the extends array. The attack requires only push access to the SCP repo (e.g., via credential theft, a compromised GitHub Actions token with write scope, or a force-push-enabled collaborator). The blast radius scales with the number of estate repos that have adopted the preset. This is supply-chain compromise of the control plane's own dependency-management surface.
findings.mitigation: Add a second GitHub rulesets entry targeting refs/tags/renovate/v* on the scp-track1 repo, applying the same protections as the existing v* ruleset: no force-push, no deletion, require linear history. This is a one-time GitHub UI or API operation and the DISPATCH-NOTE itself proposes exactly this in its remediation paragraph. Assign it to a concrete follow-up slice (e.g., 020F.1 or 020G) with a blocking tracked-forward item rather than leaving it as an untracked acceptance. As a belt-and-suspenders complement, document in ADOPT-001 §12 that adopters SHOULD pin the preset ref by its git tree hash (Renovate supports github>owner/repo//path#abc123) rather than a mutable semver tag; this limits the blast radius even if a tag is force-pushed.

findings.claim: The self-consumer renovate.json extends the preset without a #<tag> suffix, resolving to the default branch HEAD at Renovate runtime rather than to a pinned versioned tag. The DISPATCH-NOTE AC (i) checkbox claims 'Verified by SCP-self consuming the preset (vi)' but the self-consumer does not actually exercise the tagged-preset code path. AC (i) compliance is asserted but untested: the cascade validation performed in this WP is over a floating reference, not over the renovate/v1.0.0 path that adopters will use.
findings.evidence: renovate.json line 5-6: '"extends": ["github>jrnb2024/standards-control-plane//renovate/default"]' — no #<tag> suffix present. DISPATCH-NOTE AC (i): 'Preset exported via github>jrnb2024/standards-control-plane//renovate/default#<tag> (config user calls in their own renovate.json extends). Verified by SCP-self consuming the preset (vi).' The verification claim requires the self-consumer to match the format documented in AC (i), which it does not. Renovate's preset-resolution behaviour for a reference without a fragment is to use the repository's default branch HEAD at the time of the Renovate run, not a pinned release.
findings.impact: (a) Cascading template risk: if ADOPT-001 §12 shows the SCP self-consumer renovate.json as a copy-paste template (natural pattern for adopters), they receive an untagged floating reference rather than the version-pinned form required by AC (i). Any merge to SCP main would immediately change the preset config visible to those adopters on their next run, without a version bump signal. (b) Verification gap: the 020F cascade test exercises floating-main semantics, not renovate/v1.0.0 tag semantics. If the tag lookup has a different resolution behaviour or a Renovate caching/auth difference, it would not be detected. The pass/fail of the self-consumer canary does not constitute evidence that the versioned preset path works correctly.
findings.mitigation: Add '#renovate/v1.0.0' to the renovate.json extends entry immediately after the preset is tagged: 'github>jrnb2024/standards-control-plane//renovate/default#renovate/v1.0.0'. This makes the self-consumer exercise the same code path that adopters use. Alternatively, if SCP self intentionally floats on main for always-latest dogfooding, document this explicitly in renovate.json with a comment explaining the intentional deviation from the adopter template, and ensure ADOPT-001 §12 shows only the tagged form. Either way, close the AC (i) verification gap by running at least one Renovate dry-run against the renovate/v1.0.0 tag reference before declaring the slice complete.

findings.claim: The preset's automerge: false in packageRules is not enforceable against adopter overrides. Renovate evaluates packageRules in array order (last match wins on conflicting keys), and local config is appended after extends config. An adopter — or a compromised adopter PR — can silently re-enable automerge for the jrnb2024/standards-control-plane package by adding a local packageRules entry with matchPackageNames matching the SCP package and automerge: true, causing Renovate to auto-merge SCP federation primitive bumps without human review.
findings.evidence: renovate/default.json lines 14-29: packageRules entry for 'jrnb2024/standards-control-plane' sets 'automerge: false'. Renovate's configuration merging semantics: the extends array is processed in order (config:recommended first, then semantic-commits, then this preset's local rules); the consuming repo's renovate.json local config is processed last. For packageRules, Renovate concatenates all matching rules' properties in order of evaluation, with later-evaluated rules overriding earlier ones for the same key. An adopter's local renovate.json that adds {"matchPackageNames": ["jrnb2024/standards-control-plane"], "automerge": true} after the extends array would override this preset's automerge: false. There is no Renovate 'force' or 'locked' mechanism in the current preset to prevent this. The preset description notes it is supply-chain-critical but provides no enforcement documentation.
findings.impact: A careless adopter who sets automerge: true (or a malicious PR in an adopter repo) can cause Renovate to merge SCP federation primitive bumps automatically without human review. Combined with CRIT-SAFE-001 (unprotected preset tags), if an attacker force-pushes a renovate/v1.0.0 tag to a malicious commit AND an adopter has enabled automerge for the SCP package, the full attack chain (malicious preset → malicious bump PR → auto-merge) requires zero human interaction. The preset design assumes automerge: false is respected but provides no guarantee.
findings.mitigation: (a) Immediate: add a documentation block to renovate/default.json's description field and to ADOPT-001 §12 explicitly stating that adopters MUST NOT add packageRules overriding automerge for the SCP package; make this a SHOULD-audit item in the onboarding checklist. (b) Near-term: add an SCP Rego rule (SCP-R-NNN) that checks adopter renovate.json/renovate.json5 for automerge: true on the SCP package pattern; this would surface violations at the policy-check gate. (c) Aspirational: add a Renovate 'force' stanza (unsupported in standard Renovate today but available in some enterprise forks) or migrate to a manager-level lockdown if Renovate adds this capability. The mitigation at (a) is in-scope for 020H part 3; (b) is a follow-up rule addition via the RFC process.

findings.claim: The preset sets ignoreUnstable: false at root level, globally opting all adopters — including for the SCP federation primitive itself — into receiving Renovate bump proposals for pre-release and RC versions. The SCP packageRule for jrnb2024/standards-control-plane does not set ignoreUnstable: true to re-restrict the package to stable releases. This means every adopter will receive a Renovate PR proposing a bump to v1.1.0-rc.1 whenever SCP cuts an RC, and a hasty approval could install a release candidate with weakened or regressed enforcement.
findings.evidence: renovate/default.json line 13: '"ignoreUnstable": false'. The packageRules entry for jrnb2024/standards-control-plane (lines 15-28) does not include 'ignoreUnstable: true' to selectively re-restrict this package. Renovate's default for ignoreUnstable is true (ignore pre-release versions); this preset explicitly inverts that default for the entire adopter repo. The customManager matchStrings pattern at line 38 includes '(?<currentValue>v?[0-9][^\s]*)' which matches pre-release version strings like v1.1.0-rc.1. WP-SCP-020 §4 020H part 1 confirms an rc.1 tag is cut as part of the release process.
findings.impact: When SCP cuts v1.1.0-rc.1 (or any future RC), all adopters receive a Renovate bump PR to that RC version. An RC may include: a rule change that accidentally weakens enforcement (a deny → allow regression), a new input parameter with a permissive default, or a partially-implemented feature. An adopter's on-call engineer who sees 'bump SCP federation primitive to v1.1.0-rc.1' during an active incident might approve it quickly to get access to a rule fix, inadvertently installing weakened enforcement. The blast radius is the full estate. Additionally, if an attacker can influence the SCP repo to publish a malicious RC tag (e.g., via a compromised repo or a confused-deputy in the release flow), ignoreUnstable: false accelerates adoption.
findings.mitigation: Add 'ignoreUnstable': true to the jrnb2024/standards-control-plane packageRule entry to ensure adopters only receive bump proposals for stable releases of the federation primitive. Separately, evaluate whether ignoreUnstable: false at root level is intentional for all other package ecosystems — if it is only needed for specific ecosystems, scope it to those via a packageRule with matchManagers instead of setting it globally. If global pre-release tracking is intentionally desired, document the rationale and add an explicit note in ADOPT-001 §12 warning that RC bumps will appear.

findings.claim: The preset extends config:recommended (a Mend-controlled floating reference with no version pin) as its first extends entry. Renovate.com can change config:recommended's root-level settings — including automerge, schedule, or new packageRules — at any time without notice. Any such change would cascade to all adopters of this preset on their next Renovate run because the preset resolves config:recommended at runtime, not at publish time.
findings.evidence: renovate/default.json line 4: '"config:recommended"' is the first entry in the extends array. Renovate processes extends entries in order; config:recommended's settings are applied first, and this preset's explicit settings then override them for the keys it specifies. However, the preset only explicitly overrides: labels, prHourlyLimit, prConcurrentLimit, rangeStrategy, ignoreUnstable, and packageRules for the SCP package. Any config:recommended key that this preset does not explicitly set or override passes through to all adopters. Historically, Renovate has modified config:recommended multiple times (e.g., adding timezone scheduling, changing default pin strategies). There is no mechanism to pin to a specific config:recommended commit or version.
findings.impact: A future config:recommended change that (a) sets root-level automerge: true, (b) adds a schedule that conflicts with the SCP packageRule's 'at any time', (c) adds packageRules that enable automerge for ecosystem patterns, or (d) changes rangeStrategy — could silently weaken the safety properties of the SCP preset for all adopters simultaneously. Because the change arrives as a Renovate-internal preset update (not a PR against the SCP repo), it bypasses CODEOWNERS review, required-signed-commits, and tag-protection entirely. The attack surface is indirect (requires Mend's preset to change) but the consequence is estate-wide.
findings.mitigation: (a) Immediate: add explicit root-level 'automerge': false, 'prCreation': 'not-pending', and any other safety-relevant keys to the preset, so that config:recommended changes to those keys cannot override them (the preset's explicit root-level values win over extends values). (b) Medium-term: replace config:recommended with an explicit enumeration of only the specific settings the preset needs (the 'do exactly what you intend, nothing more' principle for a security-critical config surface). Document in the preset description which config:recommended behaviours are being inherited and why. (c) Add a note to the quarterly bus-factor review (2026-07-21) to check for config:recommended upstream changes since the last review.

findings.claim: The Dependabot gh-actions-minor-patch group uses patterns: ['*'] matching all GitHub Actions with no size limit. A week in which a compromised or malicious action publishes a minor or patch bump will bundle that action with all other legitimate bumps in a single PR. Reviewer attention across a 5-10-action group PR is diffuse; a malicious SHA change to one action in the group is likely to be overshadowed by the volume of benign changes.
findings.evidence: .github/dependabot.yml lines 33-39: the group 'gh-actions-minor-patch' sets 'patterns: ["*"]' covering ALL actions and 'update-types: [minor, patch]'. There is no max-open-pull-requests-limit per group, no exclusion for security-sensitive actions (e.g., actions/checkout, actions/upload-artifact), and no per-action group isolation. If 6 actions each have a minor bump in the same week, Dependabot produces one PR updating all 6 simultaneously. The 'open-pull-requests-limit: 4' at the ecosystem level limits the total number of open PRs but not the group size. Actions/checkout and actions/upload-artifact are cited in the dependabot.yml header as primary Dependabot targets and are among the most security-sensitive actions in any CI pipeline.
findings.impact: An adversary who controls a GitHub Action used in the SCP repo (directly or via a compromised maintainer) and publishes a malicious patch version can have that change bundled with 3-5 legitimate action bumps in the Monday PR. A reviewer scanning 'bump 5 actions: checkout@v4.1.1→v4.1.2, upload-artifact@v4.3.0→v4.3.1, [attacker-action]@v2.0.1→v2.0.2...' is far less likely to scrutinize the attacker-action diff than if it arrived as a standalone PR. This is a well-documented supply-chain attack pattern for bundled dependency updates.
findings.mitigation: (a) Exclude high-value actions (actions/checkout, actions/upload-artifact, and any action with write permissions) from the wildcard group and give them individual ungrouped PRs. In Dependabot this is done by adding them to a separate group or setting them as excludes. (b) Add a comment to the group entry acknowledging the bundling risk and the reviewer checklist expectation (each action SHA change must be inspected individually). (c) Consider adding a CODEOWNERS rule on .github/dependabot.yml grouping configuration (already covered by .github/** @jrnb2024) and noting in ADOPT-001 §12 that adopters should not adopt this Dependabot grouping verbatim for their own repos without per-action review hygiene.

findings.claim: The preset sets prHourlyLimit: 4 globally with no override for the vulnerabilityAlerts stanza. Under a CVE storm affecting 5 or more dependencies simultaneously, Renovate queues security-alert PRs and releases only 4 per hour, potentially leaving critical vulnerabilities unpatched for multiple hours during an active exploitation window.
findings.evidence: renovate/default.json lines 11-12: 'prHourlyLimit': 4. Lines 46-50: vulnerabilityAlerts stanza sets 'schedule: ["at any time"]' and 'automerge: false' but does NOT include a prHourlyLimit override. Renovate applies the root-level prHourlyLimit to all PR creation including vulnerability alerts unless explicitly overridden in the vulnerabilityAlerts stanza. The 2021 Log4Shell event and 2022 Spring4Shell demonstrated that coordinated CVE disclosures affecting multiple transitive dependencies can produce 10+ simultaneous security alert PRs across a single repository.
findings.impact: During a coordinated CVE event, Renovate opens 4 security PRs in hour 1, 4 in hour 2, etc. An adopter who relies on Renovate as their primary CVE notification surface may not see a critical alert PR for several hours after disclosure. This is a defense-in-depth gap (other monitoring tools should catch this independently) but for adopters relying on the preset's vulnerability alert mechanism, the throttle creates an attacker-favorable delay window.
findings.mitigation: Add 'prHourlyLimit': 0 to the vulnerabilityAlerts stanza in renovate/default.json to remove the throttle specifically for security alerts (Renovate supports per-context overrides within vulnerabilityAlerts). This is a one-line change with no other implications. Document in ADOPT-001 §12 that vulnerability-alert PRs are unthrottled and that adopters with high-security posture requirements should review prHourlyLimit for their own environments.

findings.claim: The preset's prBodyNotes includes a link to GitHub release notes at https://github.com/jrnb2024/standards-control-plane/releases/tag/v{{newValue}}. GitHub release notes are editable by any user with write access to the repo at any time after publication. A reviewer who approves a bump PR based on the release notes content could be misled if the notes are modified between PR opening and merge — or if the notes are edited post-merge to retroactively misrepresent what was in the bump.
findings.evidence: renovate/default.json lines 23-26: 'prBodyNotes': [..., 'Read the v{{newValue}} release notes at https://github.com/jrnb2024/standards-control-plane/releases/tag/v{{newValue}} before merging.']. GitHub's release editor is available to any repo collaborator with write access. The SHA pin (the authoritative source of what will execute) is not surfaced directly in the PR body alongside the release notes link, creating a potential disconnect between the narrative (release notes) and the technical fact (SHA).
findings.impact: A reviewer who reads the release notes before approving cannot rely on them as an immutable record of what the bump contains. In a social-engineering scenario: a collaborator could publish genuine release notes at bump time, obtain approvals, then edit the notes post-merge to conceal what was actually shipped. This is MIN severity because the SHA pin itself is the ground truth and the Renovate marker enforces SHA-based pinning; the release notes are advisory context only. However, using them as a pre-merge review checklist item creates a false trust anchor.
findings.mitigation: Add a note to the prBodyNotes text that the commit SHA in the uses: line is the authoritative reference, and that release notes are mutable and advisory only. Consider adding the tree hash or a content-addressed reference alongside the release notes link. In ADOPT-001 §12, instruct reviewers to verify the bump SHA against the expected tag using 'git tag -v' or 'gh release view' rather than relying on the release notes text.

findings.claim: The Dependabot schedule is fixed at Monday 09:00 Europe/London. This is a publicly observable, predictable window. An adversary who monitors SCP repo activity patterns can time a malicious release or vulnerability disclosure to arrive just before the Monday run, maximizing the chance that the compromised or urgency-framing bump lands in the gh-actions-minor-patch group alongside legitimate weekly bumps, compounding the reviewer-noise attack in MAJ-SAFE-006.
findings.evidence: .github/dependabot.yml lines 22-25: 'schedule: interval: weekly / day: monday / time: "09:00" / timezone: Europe/London'. The schedule is deterministic and makes no use of jitter or randomisation. The day and time are semantically meaningful (start-of-work-week, start-of-business-day) making them guessable without repo access. The Dependabot update schedule is not a secret; GitHub's UI exposes it and the .github/dependabot.yml file is typically public even in private repos when the config file path is known.
findings.impact: The predictability amplifies the MAJ-SAFE-006 group-bundling risk: an attacker who wants a malicious action bump to be reviewed on a busy Monday morning alongside the full batch of legitimate bumps has a reliable target window. The impact in isolation is low (MIN) but as a force multiplier on MAJ-SAFE-006 it is worth documenting. For a governance control plane that may eventually monitor high-value estate repos, a fixed public schedule is suboptimal.
findings.mitigation: Add a random offset or change the schedule to a less predictable cadence: e.g., 'schedule: random' (Dependabot supports randomised schedules) or shift to 'interval: daily' with a non-round-number time. Alternatively, accept the fixed schedule with a documented rationale and offset it from the typical disclosure timing patterns (e.g., shift from Monday morning to Wednesday afternoon to avoid aligning with patch-Tuesday disclosure patterns).

findings.claim: The preset and the renovate.json self-consumer place full trust in Mend's hosted Renovate infrastructure without any documentation of this trust assumption, its scope, or compensating controls. Renovate-opened PRs carry no cryptographic proof that they originated from the genuine Mend-hosted service. A GitHub App impersonation or Mend infrastructure compromise could open PRs that appear to be Renovate bumps but contain adversarial SHA values.
findings.evidence: renovate/default.json description (lines 3-5) and DISPATCH-NOTE.md §6 external-dependencies table entry: 'Renovate Bot hosted app | Mend | Already active on jrnb2024; org-config extends semantics verified before 020F.' The trust is implicit and undocumented in the preset artefacts themselves. CODEOWNERS and ADOPT-001 do not call out the Mend trust boundary. Renovate's GitHub App ID is public but there is no step in the adopter workflow that verifies the PR author is the genuine Mend GitHub App before review.
findings.impact: Nit severity for v1.0.0 because: (a) automerge: false means a human must approve any Renovate PR before merge; (b) the SHA pin is the safety anchor — even a spoofed PR proposing a known-malicious SHA would be visible to the reviewer; (c) Mend infrastructure compromise is a low-probability event. The finding is nit because the missing documentation does not create an active bypass vector but does leave an implicit trust assumption undocumented in a supply-chain-critical artefact.
findings.mitigation: Add a trust-boundary note to the preset description and to ADOPT-001 §12 explicitly naming Mend's Renovate hosted app as a trusted party and stating what that trust entails (Mend can open PRs proposing SHA bumps; humans must approve; Mend cannot merge without approvals). Optionally, document the GitHub App ID of the Renovate bot and encourage adopters to configure a GitHub branch-protection requirement that PR authors for automated dependency PRs must match the known App ID — GitHub supports this via required reviewers and PR author filters in rulesets.

self_reported_concerns: CRIT-SAFE-001 (unprotected renovate/v* tags) is the clearest and most severe finding; the DISPATCH-NOTE explicitly acknowledges it, which shows governance awareness, but the acknowledgement does not substitute for a tracked remediation commitment. The governance invariant 'no silent descope' requires a named future slice with a concrete timeline, not just a paragraph noting it is out-of-scope. I am reading the DISPATCH-NOTE's posture as 'acceptable deferred' rather than 'formal tracked-forward item with slice reference', which is the gap I am flagging.

MAJ-SAFE-004 (ignoreUnstable: false) may be an intentional design choice to allow the SCP team to track their own RC releases via the self-consumer renovate.json. If so, the fix is scoped: add ignoreUnstable: true only to the jrnb2024/standards-control-plane packageRule, not globally. I have no visibility into whether ignoreUnstable: false is intentional for other package ecosystems in the adopter repos; if it is, my root-level mitigation recommendation should be narrowed to the packageRule level only.

MAJ-SAFE-005 (config:recommended drift) depends on Mend's future behaviour which I cannot observe. The finding is speculative but the mechanism is real; the severity is MAJ because of the estate-wide blast radius if config:recommended gains automerge: true for any pattern this preset does not explicitly counter. I rate it MAJ rather than CRIT because it requires a third-party (Mend) action to become exploitable, not just an attacker with repo access.

I did not find evidence that the customManager regex (renovate/default.json lines 37-43) is directly bypassable via marker injection or homoglyph attack against the Renovate manager itself — the depNameTemplate is hardcoded, preventing the marker from being redirected to an attacker repo. The homoglyph risk exists at the uses: line level in adopter workflows (a reviewer might miss a unicode-lookalike repo name) but that is an adopter-PR-review problem, not a Renovate configuration bypass. I have not raised it as a formal finding given the hardcoded depNameTemplate provides a structural defence.
structured_review.summary: Slice 020F presents 1 CRIT, 5 MAJ, 3 MIN, and 1 nit safety-bypass finding against renovate/default.json, renovate.json, and .github/dependabot.yml. CRIT-SAFE-001: the renovate/v* tag series is entirely unprotected — the 020J tag-protection ruleset targets refs/tags/v* (literal v-prefix) only; an attacker with push access can silently force-push renovate/v1.0.0 to a malicious commit and cascade adversarial Renovate config to every estate adopter on their next scheduled Renovate run. CODEOWNERS guards the file, not the git tag. The DISPATCH-NOTE acknowledges this and defers it as out-of-scope; under the no-silent-descope governance invariant this must be converted to a named tracked-forward item with a concrete future-slice reference, not an unticketed acceptance-in-place. MAJ-SAFE-002: the self-consumer renovate.json extends the preset without a #<tag> suffix, floating on default-branch HEAD; the DISPATCH-NOTE AC (i) checkbox claims verification-via-self-consumption but the self-consumer does not actually exercise the versioned-preset path. MAJ-SAFE-003: automerge: false in packageRules can be silently overridden by any adopter's local packageRules entry because Renovate applies rules in order and local config post-dates extends; no enforcement mechanism exists. MAJ-SAFE-004: ignoreUnstable: false at root level globally enables RC and pre-release bump proposals for all packages including the SCP federation primitive itself, expanding the malicious-release attack surface and allowing adopters to receive PRs for RC versions that may carry weakened enforcement. MAJ-SAFE-005: config:recommended is a Mend-controlled floating dependency with no version pin; an upstream change to its root-level automerge or schedule settings would silently cascade to all preset adopters. MAJ-SAFE-006: the Dependabot gh-actions-minor-patch group uses patterns: ["*"] with no size limit, creating an unbounded bundle where a compromised action bump can hide in the noise of legitimate ones. Three MIN and one nit finding cover CVE-storm PR throttling, mutable release-note link, predictable Monday-schedule disclosure window, and undocumented Mend infrastructure trust assumption.
